column4: The section's camel dictionary form describes setting out to graze in the morning; 16:6 gives the flock's evening return and morning release as beauty and benefit, grounding its daily movement.
The section's lost-herd scene turns on an owner who cannot be found; here Moses finds two women holding their flock back until the shepherds leave, and their father is too old to herd.
The section explicitly places Moses's staff beside a herd: 20:18 says he shakes leaves down for his sheep, making the staff part of their feeding scene.
The section's dictionary sense of grazing meets the command to eat and pasture livestock, كلوا وارعوا أنعامكم; pasture is the animal's ordinary provision.
The section's grazing scene is supplied by water and trees; this verse says the rain provides drink and trees in which people pasture their animals, فيه تسيمون.
The section's herd goes out to graze; this verse says God brings water and pasture out of the earth, أخرج منها ماءها ومرعاها, the setting that feeds it.
The section treats livestock as a blessing; after 79:31's water and pasture, this verse names that provision as enjoyment for people and their cattle, متاعا لكم ولأنعامكم.
The section's herd depends on pasture; this verse names fruit and herbage, and 80:32 completes the scene by assigning them to people and their livestock.
The section calls the camel herd a blessing; after 80:31's produce and herbage, this verse says the provision is for people and their livestock, ولأنعامكم.
The section says the dictionary form النعم names camels for the good and blessing in them; 16:5 presents livestock as warmth, benefit, and food.
The section connects livestock with blessing; this verse spells out cattle's milk, many benefits, and food, making their favor perceptible.
The section's flock is an animal community under care; 36:71 says God created livestock that people own, establishing the human-animal relation behind the herd image.
The section's herd is cared for as useful livestock; this verse says animals were made manageable, with some for riding and some for food.
The section's dictionary explanation calls camels النعم because of their blessing; this verse names livestock's other benefits and drink and ends by asking for gratitude.
The section names the camel's front and rear saddle pieces; this neighboring livestock passage adds their loads carried to distant lands, another concrete use of the herd.
The section's dictionary examples include horses and their leading parts; this continuation names horses, mules, and donkeys as riding animals and adornment.
The section's 28:23 scene leaves the women waiting to water their flock; this verse says Moses waters it, then asks his Lord for whatever good He sends, joining animal care to his need.
The section calls the herd's fixed place its dictionary form مرب; this verse says every creature has provision and a known settled place and deposit, مستقرها ومستودعها.
The section pictures a herdsman who owns and leads the wandering animal; this verse says every moving creature is held by its forelock and names the Lord, آخذ بناصيتها.
The section gathers a flock into a known home under its owner; this verse calls animals communities like people and says they will be gathered to their Lord.
The section says the poor and wandering are not left without provision; this verse points to creatures unable to carry their own provision and says God provides for them and people.
The section's dictionary form هادي means the foremost animal or leader; Moses says the Lord gave each thing its form and then guided it, linking creation with directed life.
The section describes a human owner losing track of a camel; Moses says his Lord neither strays nor forgets, لا يضل ربي ولا ينسى, making divine care unlike human loss.
The section's lost owner does not know which way to go; Moses, travelling at night, hopes to find guidance at a fire, أجد على النار هدى, a concrete search for direction.
The section's lost animal is defined by not knowing its way; this verse says stars guide people through the darknesses of land and sea, لتهتدوا بها في ظلمات البر والبحر.
The section's dictionary form هادي names a leader at the head; this verse says people are guided by the stars, وبالنجم هم يهتدون, a concrete wayfinding parallel.
The section's owner searches without knowing a direction; this verse asks who guides people through the darknesses of land and sea, من يهديكم في ظلمات البر والبحر.
The section's image of the lost becoming guided is echoed by Moses, fleeing toward Midian and asking that his Lord guide him to the sound way, سواء السبيل.
The section describes a lost one receiving guidance; this verse promises that whoever follows God's guidance will neither go astray nor suffer, فمن اتبع هداي فلا يضل ولا يشقى.
The section makes ضالّ a lost animal whose owner seeks it, not a moral charge; this verse explicitly denies that Muhammad has gone astray, ما ضل صاحبكم, distinguishing the senses.
The section defines مأوى as any place a creature resorts to for shelter; these young men take refuge in a cave, أوى الفتية إلى الكهف, making refuge a chosen protection.
The section's found animal is called back into a sheltering place; the young men tell one another to take refuge in the cave, فأووا إلى الكهف, a parallel act of gathering into safety.
The section begins with a herd going out to graze; this verse names the pasture God brings forth, المرعى, using the same pasture root as the section's grazing dictionary forms.
The section's first and last herd members become the first life and Hereafter in 93:4; this verse says people prefer the nearer life, بل تؤثرون الحياة الدنيا, naming the choice that 93:4 corrects.
The section's dictionary terms for first and last extend into 93:4's Hereafter and first life; this verse says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, والآخرة خير وأبقى.
The section says God found the needy and made him self-sufficient; this verse promises to enrich poor people from His bounty, يغنهم الله من فضله.
The section links the orphan's name with goodness that can arrive late; this covenant commands good treatment of orphans, placing timely care among obligations.
The section presents orphan care as a response to someone vulnerable; this verse counts giving wealth to orphans among righteousness, making provision an act of faith.
The section's orphan is someone whose support may be delayed; this verse directs spending of good wealth to orphans among the first named recipients.
The section links the orphan to delayed goodness; this verse says setting their affairs right is best, الإصلاح لهم خير, and treats them as brothers.
The section's orphan receives shelter after being found; this verse commands guardians to hand orphans their property and forbids replacing good with bad.
The section's instruction not to oppress the orphan is made concrete here by justice toward orphan girls and the fear of wronging them.
The section names the orphan as one to whom good can arrive late; this verse requires testing until maturity and then delivering their property when judgment is sound.
The section's orphan is among those needing timely provision; this verse gives orphans present at an inheritance division a share and calls for kind words.
The section's orphan-care command meets a direct ruling here: when asked about women orphans, the verse commands justice toward them.
The section makes the orphan's delayed good visible; this verse protects orphan property until maturity and requires fair measure and weight.
The section's orphan needs what sustains him; this verse assigns orphans a share of war gains alongside other recipients.
The section's instruction against harming orphans is expressed here as a ban on approaching their property except in the best way until maturity.

The section says goodness can be slow to reach an orphan; Khidr repairs a wall hiding the two orphans' treasure so they can retrieve it when they mature, a provision deliberately kept for their future.
The section names the orphan among those vulnerable to delayed provision; this verse includes orphans among the recipients of shared wealth so it does not circulate only among the rich.
The section joins orphanhood with need; this verse describes feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food oneself.
The section's orphan is not to be oppressed; this verse directly rebukes failure to honor the orphan, and 89:18 adds neglect of feeding the poor.
The section's orphan receives kindness after a vulnerable beginning; this verse specifies feeding an orphan who is a relative, يتيما ذا مقربة, as a difficult good deed.
The section commands that the orphan not be oppressed; this verse identifies repelling the orphan as a mark of denial, a direct reversal of shelter and care.
The section's horses return when called by their keeper; this verse likens disbelievers to one calling animals that hear only cries and calls, showing a voice that reaches ears without understanding.
The section's animal is lost but can be led home; this verse compares the heedless to cattle and says they are more astray, بل هم أضل, reversing the animal's relation to guidance.
The section's flock responds to a keeper's call; this verse compares unreasoning people to cattle and calls them more astray in the way, بل هم أضل سبيلا.
The section's lost camel has an owner who searches and restores it to shelter; at the Hour, prized camels are left unattended, العشار عطلت, a direct reversal of care.
The section's image is a vulnerable orphan finally received into care; this verse reverses that care by warning that those who consume orphans' property unjustly consume fire.

The section's lost animal cannot find its direction; this verse says the opponents have strayed and cannot find a way, ضلوا فلا يستطيعون سبيلا, a moral use of the same root set against the physical image.
The section develops shelter as taking in a vulnerable orphan or stray; this verse names believers who gave shelter and support to the emigrants, آووا ونصروا, as a communal form of care.
The section's dictionary meaning of shelter is a creature's refuge; this verse again describes believers who sheltered and aided the emigrants, extending refuge to people in need.
The section's lost creature is not ownerless but received into a home; this verse describes the Medinan helpers who made a home for the emigrants and preferred them over themselves.
The section defines مأوى as a place of refuge; this verse says God made homes from livestock hides and furnishings from their wool, hair, and fur, tying animal life to shelter.
The section's herd depends on pasture; this next verse shows that pasture drying into dark stubble, adding the passing cycle of the ground on which it feeds.
The section's source root ء خ ر moves from the rear of a herd to the Hereafter; this verse pairs the Hereafter and first life as belonging to God, للآخرة والأولى.
The section's first and last positions echo its surah's first-life/Hereafter contrast; this verse says both the Hereafter and the first life belong to God, فلله الآخرة والأولى.
The section uses first and last for positions in a herd; this verse applies those same dictionary forms to God, الأول والآخر, moving the sequence's terms beyond any created order.

The section's first, last, advancing, and lagging members give spatial force to its root ء خ ر; this verse speaks of what a person sent ahead and left behind, بما قدم وأخر, transferring sequence to deeds.
The section's root ʿ-y-l names a needy person as well as one left without direction; this verse names fear of poverty, عيلة, and promises enrichment from God.
The section's orphan is a named recipient of care; this verse includes orphans among those to whom believers must do good.
The section connects God's finding and enriching the needy to care for the orphan; this verse says people read expanded provision as honor, a belief the following orphan rebuke corrects.
The section joins need with later provision; this verse says people read restricted provision as humiliation, and 89:17 answers that the orphan is the one they fail to honor.
The section's orphan is part of the vulnerable flock of people needing care; this verse names the failure to urge feeding the poor, completing 89:17's orphan rebuke.
The section connects care with what reaches the vulnerable; this verse names feeding on a day of hunger, and 90:15 specifies the near orphan as a recipient.
The section joins the orphan's delayed kindness with the poor person's need; this verse names a destitute person in misery, continuing 90:15's account of whom care reaches.
The section's orphan-care image includes provision for vulnerable people; following 107:2, this verse condemns failure to urge feeding the poor.
